title: Agent Design Guidelines
about: The core file for the Agent Design Guidelines. The website, patterns.md and the Discovery Engine plugin all read from this file. Edit patterns here only. Pattern and principle ids never change; names, text and order can.

groups.name: Before the agent acts
groups.summary: Agree on what the agent may do, and when.

groups.name: While the agent acts
groups.summary: Show the work, and keep people in control of every decision.

groups.name: After the agent acts
groups.summary: Say honestly what happened, and keep a record anyone can follow.

groups.name: Over time
groups.summary: Let trust grow with a track record.

patterns.name: Agent disclosure
patterns.rule: Clear from the first interaction which agent is doing the work, on every task, proposal and message.
intro: Show that the user is working with an agent from the first interaction, and on everything the agent does. The AI Act (article 50) requires this, and a note in the terms and conditions isn’t enough.
Use the same marker everywhere, and a role name instead of a person’s name or face.
look_for: The agent named at the start of the work
A plain role name, like “Payroll agent”, never a person’s name or face
The agent named on every task, proposal and message
A way to see what the agent does and what it’s based on
patterns.do: A banner says the user is working with the Payroll agent, and the badge explains what it does. Every proposal says who proposed it.
patterns.avoid: A one-time “AI filled this” banner, or AI mentioned only in the terms and conditions.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including suggestions, answers and work status.

items.marker: A banner names the agent, and the badge explains it
items.what: At the top of the payroll run, a banner tells the user they are working with the Payroll agent and that money never moves without their approval. When clicked, the badge reveals what the agent does and what data it uses.

items.marker: Each running task names its agent
items.what: A list of current work, with each line starting with the agent doing it. A spinner shows what’s running now, and finished tasks move down with a tick and when they finished. The agent is named at all stages.

items.marker: The proposing agent is named next to the decision
items.what: The Absence agent proposes changing an employee payslip under the Sick Pay Act. ‘Proposed by Absence agent’ stays next to Accept, Edit and Reject, and is still there after the user decides.

items.marker: Messages show who drafted it and who sent it
items.what: A question to a client about a purchase is marked ‘Drafted by Client agent, sent by you’. When the client replies, the Bookkeeping agent proposes how to book it, and that proposal is labelled as the agent’s too.

patterns.name: Autonomy levels
patterns.rule: A level per task, from Off to Auto, set by the user. Pay never runs on Auto.
intro: A named setting, such as Off, Suggest, Ask first or Auto, chosen separately for each task, so low-risk work can run alone while high-risk work waits for approval.
look_for: A level per task: Off, Suggest, Ask first or Auto
The current level visible, with what the agent will do
Different levels for different areas of the same agent
The level shown on each action in the log
Pay, filings and salary changes never run on Auto
patterns.do: Collecting time on Auto, exception checks on Ask first, and the payment file to the bank never on Auto, each visible on screen.
patterns.avoid: One on/off switch for the whole product.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including levels per task, permissions per area and the level behind each action.

items.marker: Each task has its own level, and pay never runs on Auto
items.what: Payroll tasks, each set to Off, Suggest, Ask first or Auto, with a line saying what the agent will do at that level. The user can change each level, but Auto can’t be chosen for the payment file to the bank.

items.marker: One agent, a different permission per area
items.what: The Bookkeeping agent is allowed to work in the ledger, must ask before emailing customers, and is kept out of bank payments and payroll. When it tries to send overdue reminders, it stops and asks first. The user can change each permission, or switch the whole agent between Ask, Plan and Agent mode.

items.marker: The log shows the level behind each action
items.what: Each line in the activity log names the agent, what it did and the level it ran at. Actions that needed approval also show who approved them, so it’s clear afterwards what the agent did on its own.

patterns.name: Triggers
patterns.rule: Starts on its own on a date or an event, says what started it, and shows what’s next.
intro: The agent starts on its own when a date arrives or something happens, such as a client replying, and reports what it did. The user can see what will run next, and pause it.
look_for: The trigger in plain words: “when time reporting closes”
What started the run, shown at the top
A way to pause a trigger, or a single task, before it runs
What runs next, and when
patterns.do: The run starts when time reporting closes and says so at the top. The next tasks are listed by date, each with a way to pause it.
patterns.avoid: Work that only starts when someone remembers to press “Run agent”.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including schedules, events and the start of a run.

items.marker: Each trigger says when it runs, and can be paused
items.what: Agents start on their own: on a date, every month, or when a client replies. Each line names the agent and shows what it did last and when it runs next. The user can pause a trigger with the switch without deleting it.

items.marker: The run opens with what started it
items.what: The Payroll agent started on its own when time reporting closed, and says so at the top, with the time and date. It then collects from each source one by one, and ends with the date of the next run.

items.marker: What the agent does next, with a pause on each task
items.what: The list opens with what started the run, then shows the agent’s next tasks by date. The user can pause any task the agent does on its own before it runs. The payment file is marked ‘Waits for you’ because it never goes without approval.

patterns.name: Suggestions
patterns.rule: Prepares the change and offers it. Nothing happens until the user confirms.
intro: The agent prepares a change, or suggests the next step based on what is in the books. Nothing happens until the user confirms.
look_for: The change prepared, with what it will do
One clear way to confirm, and a way to say not now
Nothing happens until the user confirms
A preview of anything that will be sent
patterns.do: The agent proposes adding vacation pay to a final salary, shows the salary now next to the proposal, and changes nothing until the user confirms.
patterns.avoid: The agent acts first and tells the user afterwards.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a single change to a whole payroll run prepared for approval.

items.marker: Offered, awaiting confirmation
items.what: An employee is leaving with unused vacation days, so the Payroll agent proposes adding vacation pay to the final salary. It shows the salary now next to the proposal, and nothing changes until the user confirms. The user can undo it afterwards.

items.marker: The agent offers to match receipts, and the user confirms
items.what: The agent finds receipts in the inbox for card payments that are missing one, and offers to match them. Nothing happens until the user confirms. After matching, the user checks the matches and books them, or undoes the matching.

items.marker: The next step is suggested where the work is
items.what: An invoice is late, and the Invoice agent suggests sending a friendly reminder, as this client usually pays soon after one. The user can preview the exact email before sending it, and it’s marked as drafted by the agent and sent by the user.

items.marker: Prepared, not sent
items.what: The Payroll agent prepares the bank file, payslips, journal and employer declaration, and sends nothing until the user approves. Each action then ticks off as it goes out.

patterns.name: Live progress
patterns.rule: Progress per source or step, with what was found and the rule behind it.
intro: A progress indicator and running feed while the agent works, with the rule or confidence behind each step and links to its sources. The user can pause the run at any time.
look_for: Progress per source or step
What was found, and the rule or confidence behind each step
Named states: working, waiting, paused, done
A way to pause the run
Answers that link to their sources
patterns.do: Each source is marked as collecting, then done, with a short note on what was found. The user can pause the run at any time.
patterns.avoid: A spinner, then a result. Or a bare percentage.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from progress per source to named steps that can be paused.

items.marker: Progress per source, with what was found
items.what: The Payroll agent collects time, absence, employee changes, tax and advances one source at a time. Each one is marked as collecting, then done, with a short note on what it found, such as a question to answer or a change to review.

items.marker: A running count, with the reason behind each step
items.what: While the Reconciliation agent matches bank lines, a progress bar and count show how far it has come, and finished steps appear in a feed. Each step has a tag with the rule or confidence it used. Clicking the tag shows the reason.

items.marker: Each step has a named state
items.what: The Close agent works through the month-end close step by step, and each step is marked as working, waiting, paused or done. When it needs approval, it waits for the user, who can also pause the run at any time.

items.marker: Answers link to sources
items.what: The user asks whether a price on an invoice is right, and the Contract agent shows that it’s checking before it answers. The answer marks each number with a source, and clicking a marker shows the contract clause or invoice line it came from.

patterns.name: Failure disclosure
patterns.rule: What failed, why, what’s still on track and what to do next.
intro: When the agent can’t finish, it says so plainly: what failed, why, what did not happen and what the user can do next, including when it found nothing. It never covers a failure with a confident summary.
look_for: The failure named plainly, like “Bank file rejected”
The cause, in the user’s terms
What didn’t happen, and what is still on track
A way forward: fix it, retry, or hand it to a person
Empty results said as empty, with where the agent looked
The outcome recorded in the log, whichever way forward is chosen
patterns.do: “Bank file rejected. One payment is missing a bank code. No payments were sent.” Then: fix it and resend, send the other payments, or hand it to a colleague.
patterns.avoid: “Something went wrong.” A failure that looks like a normal result, or a run that keeps retrying forever.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a single failed payslip to a whole run that stops.

items.marker: One part fails, the rest stays on track
items.what: One payslip couldn’t be delivered because the new employee hasn’t activated the app. The Payroll agent says why, confirms that salaries and the other payslips went out, and recommends a way forward. The user’s choice waits a few seconds so it can be undone, and the agent can learn from the failure.

items.marker: The failure is named, with what didn’t happen
items.what: The bank rejects a payment file because one payment is missing a bank code. The agent names the failure, gives the cause and says no payments were sent. The user can fix it and resend, send the other payments, or hand it to a colleague.

items.marker: Nothing found, and where it looked
items.what: The user asks the Invoice agent for a delivery note, and it says plainly that none was found. It lists where it searched and where it couldn’t search, then offers to ask the supplier or a colleague.

items.marker: A stopped run, said plainly
items.what: A payroll run can’t calculate tax, so the agent stops. It says where it stopped, why, what wasn’t done and what it will try next. The user can also choose to continue with last year’s tax tables for now.

patterns.name: Exceptions
patterns.rule: Routine work in one line. Only what needs judgement is listed, with the reason.
intro: Routine items are handled automatically and summarised in one line. Only the items that need judgement are listed, each with the reason it was flagged and a proposal.
look_for: A count of what needs the user
One card per item: problem, proposal, reason
What the agent did on its own, with the rule that allowed it
Bulk actions only for the easy ones
An empty state when nothing needs the user
patterns.do: Routine invoices summed up in one line, and only the ones that need judgement listed, each with the problem, the proposal and the reason.
patterns.avoid: Alerts for everything, and no proposal.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a queue with reasons, bulk actions and an agent inbox.

items.marker: Routine work in one line, exceptions listed with the reason
items.what: Most of today’s supplier invoices were approved by the Invoice agent, and that’s summed up in one line. The two that need judgement are listed separately. Opening one shows the problem, the agent’s proposal and the rule that flagged it, and the user decides.

items.marker: What needs the user, and what the agent did alone
items.what: The overview leads with what the agent couldn’t settle: a frozen payment after a bank account change, and a question about a sick day. Each has the reason and a way to decide. Below, what the agent did on its own is listed with the rule that allowed it.

items.marker: Easy exceptions together, risky ones on their own
items.what: Card payments missing a receipt can all be matched in one go, because the agent found receipts with the same amount and date. A payment to a new bank account is left out of the bulk action, and the user has to check it separately.

items.marker: One inbox for what every agent needs
items.what: Each agent posts what it needs from the user, newest first, like email. The list gets shorter as the user marks items done, and says so when nothing needs them.

patterns.name: Review and approve
patterns.rule: Each change shown as before and after, to accept, edit, reject or hand over.
intro: Each suggested change is shown as a before-and-after, with its reason and rule, and three actions: accept, edit or reject. The user can always edit the change themselves.
Nothing is saved until every change is decided.
look_for: Before and after, with the reason and rule
Accept, edit and reject on each change
High-stakes fields, like a bank account, marked
Nothing saved until every change is decided
A choice whether the agent learns from an edit
patterns.do: A different VAT code is suggested for a foreign supplier’s invoice, with the current booking next to the proposal and the rule behind it. The user accepts, rejects or edits it before anything is booked.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a single change to a draft the user edits before sending.

items.marker: A suggested change, shown as before and after
items.what: The Bookkeeping agent suggests a different VAT code for an invoice from a foreign supplier, showing the current booking next to the proposal, with the reason and rule. The user can accept, reject, or edit it by picking another account before anything is booked.

items.marker: Accept, edit, reject or hand over
items.what: A payment was frozen after an employee’s bank account changed. The case shows what happened, which rule matched, and the agent’s proposal next to what happens now. If the user edits the proposal, they choose whether the agent learns from the change.

items.marker: Each change gets its own decision
items.what: The Supplier agent proposes updating a supplier’s bank account, payment terms and address. Each change is accepted or rejected on its own, and the bank account is marked as high stakes. Nothing is saved until every change is decided and the user saves.

items.marker: The user can edit the draft before sending
items.what: The Invoice agent drafts a payment reminder. The user can send it as it is, edit the text in place, or go back to the agent’s draft. Once sent, it shows that the agent drafted it and the user sent it.

patterns.name: Clarifying questions
patterns.rule: One specific question with a best guess, while the rest of the work carries on.
intro: The agent recognises when it’s uncertain and asks a specific question instead of guessing or flagging the whole item. The question comes with its best guess, the alternatives and what it will do with the user’s answer.
look_for: One specific question, about the part the agent doesn’t know
Its best guess, and why
What each answer will do
The rest of the work carrying on while the question waits
An option to remember the answer next time
patterns.do: “An employee was off with no absence reason. Sick leave, vacation or unpaid leave? It affects sick pay.” With sick leave marked as the best guess.
patterns.avoid: Booking unpaid leave straight away, or flagging the whole payslip for review.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a single question with a best guess to a question that doesn’t hold up the rest of the run.

items.marker: One question, with a best guess and what each answer does
items.what: An employee was off for a day with no absence reason. The Absence agent asks whether it was sick leave, vacation or unpaid leave, marks its best guess and why, and shows what each answer will do to pay. The user can answer, or ask the employee instead.

items.marker: A question about pay, with a guess the agent can learn from
items.what: A sick day overlaps a booked vacation day, and the manager’s note is unclear. The Payroll agent asks because the answer changes pay, and adds its guess. If the user answers differently, they can let the agent learn from it, and it still asks next time.

items.marker: One question doesn’t hold up the rest
items.what: Payroll keeps running for everyone else while one question waits. Only one line on one payslip is missing. When the user answers, that payslip is finished too.

patterns.name: Escalation
patterns.rule: Stops at the edge of the rules and hands the case to a named person, with what was checked.
intro: When the agent reaches the edge of the rules, or something fails, it prepares what it can, stops, and hands the case to a named person with what it checked, what failed and why it’s theirs.
Failure disclosure tells the user what went wrong. Escalation hands the case to the person who should decide, for example an accountant for whether a cost is an asset or a repair.
look_for: A named person, not a queue
What was checked, and why it’s their call
The case handed over with its data, rule and proposal
A way to take it back
patterns.do: A judgement call handed to an accountant with what the agent checked and drafts for both options.
patterns.avoid: The case parked in a suspense account, or the agent guessing.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a hand-over with what was checked to a stop when something fails.

items.marker: The case goes to a named person, with what was checked
items.what: An invoice could be booked as an asset or as a repair, and the choice is a judgement call. The Close agent prepares drafts for both, stops, and hands the case to an accountant with what it checked and why it’s their call. The accountant takes the case and decides.

items.marker: Handed to a colleague or the client, with the full case
items.what: When unsure about a frozen payment, the user hands the case to a colleague or to the client. It goes with its data, rule and the agent’s proposal, and the payment stays frozen in the meantime. The user can take it back.

items.marker: It stops, and offers ways forward
items.what: The Invoice agent can’t read an invoice attachment, so it can’t suggest a VAT code. It says what’s missing and offers three ways forward: enter the code yourself, ask a colleague, or upload a readable copy.

patterns.name: Undo
patterns.rule: Undo where the result shows up, changes until approval, and a warning before what can’t be undone.
intro: Anything the agent did can be reversed right where it shows up, for as long as that is still possible, and the agent says before it acts what can’t be undone. An undo is logged like the action.
Payments, for example, can’t be undone once they leave the bank, so the agent says so before they go.
look_for: Undo where the result shows up, and how long it’s possible
Changes possible until the user approves
What can’t be undone, said before it acts
A correction offered when something can’t be unsent
Every undo logged like the action
patterns.avoid: Undo that’s only available in the log, far from where the change shows up.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from undo on a single result to a log where every change can be undone.

items.marker: Undo sits on the result, with how long it’s possible
items.what: The Reminder agent has sent a payment reminder, and the Undo button sits right on it, with how long it’s still possible. Undoing recalls the reminder before it reaches the client, and the undo is logged like the send.

items.marker: Changeable until the user approves
items.what: The agent sets payday by the client’s rule, and the user can move it for this month only, until they approve. The change can also be suggested to the client as a new rule. Once approved, payday is locked.

items.marker: It says what can’t be undone before it acts
items.what: Before scheduling supplier payments, the Close agent says they can’t be undone once they leave the bank, and until when they can still be stopped. The user schedules them and can stop them until the bank file is sent. After that, the only way back is a refund.

items.marker: Every change can be undone where it’s listed
items.what: A reminder is held for a few seconds before it sends, with Undo on it. In the list of today’s changes, each one can be undone right there. What can’t be unsent offers a correction instead, and every undo becomes a line of its own.

patterns.name: Audit trail
patterns.rule: A plain-language record of every step, with who did it: the agent or the user.
intro: A time-stamped record of every run: what the agent read, what it changed, which rules it used and who reviewed the result.
Write it so an auditor or the tax authority could follow it.
look_for: Every step, in order, in plain sentences
Who did each step: the agent or the user
Why the agent acted, one click away
A filter by who did it
Undo from the log
patterns.do: A run logged step by step: what started it, what it read, what it posted and with which rules, and who reviewed it.
patterns.avoid: Raw system logs, and no undo.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from a run logged step by step to a shared timeline the user can undo from.

items.marker: Each step of the run, in order
items.what: The Reconciliation agent’s run is logged step by step: what started it, what it read, what it posted and with which rules, what it sent for review, and who reviewed it. Clicking an entry shows the details.

items.marker: Every step in plain language, with who did it
items.what: The run log lists every step, newest first, and says whether the agent or the user did it. The user can filter by either, and open an agent step to see why it acted.

items.marker: Agent and user steps in one timeline
items.what: The agent’s steps and the user’s own steps sit in one timeline, and the user’s steps carry their initials. The user can filter by who did it, and undo the bank file straight from the log.

patterns.name: Recap
patterns.rule: The outcome and what’s left, a regular summary, and a brief when the user comes back.
intro: A regular summary with concrete numbers, such as time saved, issues caught and items handled without edits. When the user comes back to a long-running job, the agent first tells them what happened while they were away and what needs them now.
look_for: The outcome first, then what still needs the user
What the agent handled on its own, and what it caught
What it got wrong or wasn’t sure about
The details, one click away
patterns.do: “October payroll is done.” Then what still needs the user, the month in numbers, and the reports the agent sends on its own.
patterns.avoid: A count of messages sent, or a list of every notification since the user was last in.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, from the end of a payroll run to a brief when the user comes back.

items.marker: The run ends with the outcome, and what’s left
items.what: The recap leads with the outcome, then what still needs the user, the month in numbers, and the reports the agent sends on its own. Releasing a held payment asks the user to confirm first, because it can’t be stopped once it’s sent.

items.marker: A weekly recap with what the agents did
items.what: A weekly card shows time saved, issues caught, how much was accepted without edits, and where the agents were weaker. The user can switch week, or click a figure to see what’s behind it.

items.marker: A brief on what happened while the user was away
items.what: After a weekend away, the user first sees one line about what was handled and what needs them. The details, what needs them and what’s done, are one click away, and each item can be handled from there.

items.marker: A long thread opens with a short summary
items.what: The Invoice agent sums up a long thread with a supplier in a few points. Each point links to the message it came from, and clicking it highlights that message.

patterns.name: Earned autonomy
patterns.rule: Offers to do more after a track record, and steps back after corrections.
intro: After several approvals without changes, the agent offers to do that action on its own. After corrections or reversals, it steps back and asks again.
Reminders, matching and coding can earn their way to Auto. Pay, filings and salary changes never do.
look_for: A track record of approvals without changes
An offer to do more after a set number of approvals without changes, with a way to say no
A step back after corrections, with the reason
Levels stepped through one at a time
Things that never move up: pay, filings, salary changes
patterns.do: After enough approvals without changes the agent offers to do more, and after corrections it steps back and says why.
patterns.avoid: It always asks, or it runs fully automatic from day one.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including an offer at a threshold, a step back after corrections and levels that can be stepped through.

items.marker: It offers to do more after a track record
items.what: Each approved reminder is tracked. Once enough have been approved without changes, the Reminder agent offers to send reminders on its own, and says how to switch it back. The user can accept or keep it asking.

items.marker: It steps back after corrections
items.what: The Account agent codes invoices on its own. When the user corrects it twice, it moves itself back to Suggest, says why, and says what it takes to earn the level back.

items.marker: More autonomy offered, based on months of work
items.what: The user’s time per run falls month by month as the agent takes on more. Based on its record, the agent offers to decide routine exceptions on its own. The level per task also shows where it stepped back after being corrected.

items.marker: Levels the user can step through
items.what: Everyone starts at Off. The user steps up one level at a time, through Suggest and Ask first to Auto, when the agent has earned it, and can step down at any time. Pay, filings and salary changes never move up.

principles.name: Lead with the work, not a prompt
principles.statement: The agent brings what needs attention. Nobody should have to know what to ask.

in_practice.text: The home screen is the recommendation. Most viewing starts there, not in search.
Add a location to an event and it tells you when it’s time to leave, based on traffic. Nobody has to ask.
A weekly report arrives on its own, summarising how you used your device over the past seven days.
The tax return arrives pre-filled. If it’s right, you approve it by text message.
Nudges you well ahead of VAT deadlines, and lists what still needs doing before you file.
Requests for missing receipts, and the reminders that follow, go out on their own.

details.heading: The work comes to the user
paragraphs: An empty chat box asks the user to know what to do, what to ask and how to phrase it. A proactive agent turns that around. It watches the books, starts when something happens, and arrives with the work prepared: what changed, what it proposes and what needs a decision. The user reviews instead of starting from a blank page.

points.text: Recognising a good proposal is easier than describing what you want. One look and a confirm replaces several rounds of typing and refining.
An agent that is watching notices the late invoice, the missing absence reason or the changed bank account, even when nobody thought to ask.

points.term: It fits the work the user already does
points.text: Payroll, invoicing, VAT and closing follow a rhythm of dates, deadlines and events. The agent can follow that rhythm too, so the work is ready when the user needs it.

details.heading: When a prompt is the better choice
paragraphs: Chat is still the right tool when the user knows something the agent can’t predict:

points.text: One-off analyses, unusual scenarios or “what if” questions that don’t follow a pattern.
Someone who only logs in now and then, such as a manager looking up a figure. They have no routine for the agent to follow, so asking is quicker.
“Why did this employee’s net pay drop?”, “What does this rule mean?” The user is looking for understanding, not a task done.

details.heading: Many agents need both
paragraphs: Lead with the work for routine tasks, and keep a prompt available for everything else. The principle is about where the user starts, not about removing chat.
details.ask: If the user opened the product and typed nothing, would they still see what needs them today?

principles.name: The higher the stakes, the tighter the control
principles.statement: Routine work runs alone. Money, pay and filings wait for a person.

in_practice.text: Tap freely for small amounts. Above €50, or after a few taps in a row, the PIN is required.
In agent mode, it asks for permission before any action of consequence.
Automatic reconciliation is switched on per bank account, and acts only when highly confident.
Filing waits for you. A text message can only approve the return as it is; any change goes through the online service.
Custom agents make proposals, but can’t change a client’s books on their own.

details.heading: Match the control to what’s at stake
paragraphs: One level of control for everything fails in one of two ways. If everything needs approval, the user spends their day confirming routine work and the agent saves no time. If nothing does, one wrong payment or filing can undo months of trust. Setting control by risk avoids both.

points.text: Routine work runs on its own, so the user’s attention goes to the decisions that need judgement.
When only a few things need a yes, the user reads them properly. Asking about everything trains the user to click without looking.
What the agent does alone can be undone. What can’t be undone waits for a person.

details.heading: How to judge what’s at stake
paragraphs: The same agent can do low-risk and high-risk work in one run. Judge each action on its own:

points.text: A booking can be corrected. A salary payment or a submitted tax return can’t.
Money to the bank, a message to a customer and a report to the tax authority all reach someone outside.

points.term: How much, and for how many?
points.text: A large amount, or a change that affects every employee, needs more care than a single small correction.

points.term: Is it someone’s money or personal data?
points.text: Salaries, bank account details and absence reasons affect real people directly.

details.heading: Control is a scale, not a switch
paragraphs: Between doing everything alone and asking about everything, there are levels: suggest, ask first, act and report. The same task can also use different levels depending on the case. Small, familiar invoices are matched automatically, while unusual or large ones wait for the user. When the agent is unsure, it moves to a tighter level on its own, never a looser one.
details.ask: If the agent got this wrong, who would notice, and could it be fixed before it mattered?

principles.name: Never hide the agent, never hide the reason
principles.statement: Always labelled as an agent, and always showing why.

in_practice.text: Rows like “Because you watched…” say why each title is recommended.
Review summaries are labelled as AI-generated, and each theme opens the reviews behind it.
When an email can’t be delivered, Gmail tells you why and what you can do about it.
Each auto-reconciled line says how: rule, match, memory or prediction.
A Rule label shows when a bank rule categorised a transaction.
Every automated categorisation gets a confidence score, and each transaction’s activity log shows what changed, when and by whom.

details.heading: Trust starts with knowing who did what
paragraphs: Users check work differently depending on who did it. When they can see that a booking, a message or a payslip change came from the agent, they know what to look at and how closely. When they find out afterwards, even a correct result feels like something was hidden from them.

points.text: The AI Act (article 50) requires that the user is told when they’re dealing with AI, from the first interaction.
When an auditor, a client or a colleague asks who made a change, the answer is on the screen and in the log.
A plain role name like “Payroll agent”, never a person’s name or face, makes clear that this is software that follows rules and can be wrong.

details.heading: A reason the user can check
paragraphs: Saying that the agent did something is only half of it. The user also needs to see why, in terms they can verify:

points.text: The time report, contract clause or bank line the decision is based on, one click away.
“Matched on amount and reference” or “Collective agreement, overtime rate” tells the user what to check if it looks wrong.
A confident match and a best guess shouldn’t look the same.
One line next to the result, with the details available on request.

details.heading: Clear, not noisy
paragraphs: Showing the agent doesn’t mean shouting about it. Use the same quiet marker everywhere, so users learn to recognise it without reading it. Keep the reason for routine items one click away, and show it upfront when something is unusual or high-stakes. A screen where everything is labelled and explained at full volume hides what matters just as well as one that explains nothing.
details.ask: For any line in the books, could the user tell whether the agent did it, and why?

principles.name: Control is always one step away
principles.statement: Accept, edit, undo or take over, in one step.

in_practice.text: With Undo send, every email waits 5 seconds by default, up to 30, with Undo right there.
Copilot’s drafts come with Keep it, Regenerate and Discard, so nothing is added without you.
In agent mode, you can interrupt, take over the browser, or stop the task at any point.
When its AI agent hands a chat to a person, the person gets a summary of the conversation, so the customer doesn’t have to start again.
Change an account code or tax rate right on the Reconciled page, or remove and redo a match.
Undo on a categorised bank transaction sends it back to For review, and automations can be paused or edited at any time.
A submitted payroll can be cancelled until the bank account is debited, with a Cancel button right in the pay history.

details.heading: Control is what makes letting go possible
paragraphs: Users hand over work when they know they can step back in. If changing the agent’s work means hunting through settings, asking support or starting over, they hold on to everything themselves, and the agent saves no time. When control is always within reach, they can let the agent do more.

points.text: Users try Auto on more tasks when they know a mistake takes one step to fix.
A wrong proposal fixed in place costs seconds. One found after the payroll run costs a correction, an explanation and some trust.
An edit to the agent’s proposal shows what the user knows that the agent doesn’t, and the agent can learn from it.

details.heading: Five ways to step in
paragraphs: Every piece of agent work should offer the controls that fit it:

points.text: One clear action, with what will happen once the user confirms.
Change the proposal where it is, without starting over or rewriting it from scratch.
Reverse it right where the result shows up, for as long as that is still possible.
Stop the agent for now, and let it carry on from where it left off when the user is ready.
Stop the agent and continue by hand, with everything it has done so far.

details.heading: Close at hand, not in the way
paragraphs: Controls belong next to the work they affect, not in a settings page or at the end of a log. They should be in the same place every time, so users find them without searching. Being close doesn’t mean interrupting, though: the controls wait quietly until they’re needed. And there should never be a point where the agent is running and the user can’t stop it.
details.ask: Wherever the agent is working, how many steps would it take the user to stop it or change what it did?

principles.name: Flag what’s new, not just what’s wrong
principles.statement: The unusual case is the one that matters.

in_practice.text: “You don’t often get email from…” appears when someone new writes.
Before a euro transfer, your bank checks the payee’s name against the account and tells you if it doesn’t match.
Before deep research starts, it may ask a few questions to confirm your goals, and shows a plan you can change.
In payroll, Copilot points out pay that looks different from usual, so you can check it before anyone is paid.
Bank transactions that match nothing are marked “Need your review” instead of being booked.
Control Center sends the accounting firm only the exceptions that need their expertise.
Low-confidence categorisations go to a checklist for review instead of being posted.

details.heading: Valid isn’t the same as normal
paragraphs: Most checks look for errors: a missing field, a wrong format, a sum that doesn’t add up. But the cases that cost the most often pass every check. A supplier’s bank account changes, an invoice is much larger than usual, or a new employee is paid for the first time. Nothing is technically wrong, yet each one deserves a second look.

points.text: A changed bank account on a familiar supplier is one of the most common ways money goes missing, and it passes every format check.
A new employee, a new supplier or a new rule hasn’t been through a normal run yet, so nobody knows whether it works.
When what’s new is always flagged, users can trust everything that isn’t flagged, and spend less time checking it.

details.heading: What counts as new
paragraphs: The agent compares each item with what it has seen before:

points.text: A new bank account, address or tax setting on someone the agent already knows.
The first invoice from a supplier, or the first payslip for an employee.
An amount, date or frequency that’s unusual for this supplier, employee or customer.
New tax tables, a changed collective agreement or a new law that applies for the first time.

details.heading: New isn’t wrong
paragraphs: A flag should say what changed and what it’s compared with: the old bank account next to the new one, or the usual amount next to this one. It shouldn’t block the work or sound like an error. The user confirms it, and the agent remembers, so the same change isn’t flagged again next time. If everything is flagged as new, nothing stands out, so keep flags for what is new to this case.
details.ask: If something in this run had never happened before, would the user know?

principles.name: Autonomy is earned, not granted
principles.statement: The agent proves itself run by run, and steps back when it’s wrong.

in_practice.text: Apps ask before using your location, you can allow it just once, and apps that use it in the background are checked again later, with a map of where.
Copilot helps with day-to-day work, and Autopilot takes over set processes under the team’s supervision. Firms switch automations on client by client.
Bank rules categorise transactions for you to review first. Booking them automatically is a separate choice, per rule.
Switched on per bank account; “memory” decisions are based on how you reconciled similar transactions before.
Each confirmation or correction applies right away to similar transactions, for that client, the firm and across Digits.

details.heading: Trust is built, not switched on
paragraphs: An agent that runs on Auto from the first day asks for blind trust. One that always asks never saves the user time. Earned autonomy sits between the two: the agent starts by suggesting, shows what it can do on the user’s own work, and takes on more as it proves itself.

points.term: Proof from the user’s own work
points.text: The track record comes from their clients, rules and data, not from a demo or a promise.
Each step up is small, so the user never has to trust more than they’ve already seen.
The agent can offer to do more, but the user decides when it happens.

details.heading: How autonomy is earned
paragraphs: Earning works the same way for every task:

points.text: Approvals without changes are counted for each task, so doing well on reminders says nothing about pay.
When the track record is good enough, the agent offers the next level and shows why. The user can say yes, not now, or never.
From Suggest to Ask first, then to Auto, never skipping a step.
Corrections or reversals move the task back a level, and the agent says why.

details.heading: Some things never earn Auto
paragraphs: A track record doesn’t change what’s at stake. Pay, filings and salary changes always wait for a person, however many times the agent has got them right. Reminders, matching and coding can earn their way to Auto. Trust also takes longer to build than to lose: one serious mistake should count for more than many good runs.
details.ask: Could the user see why the agent is allowed to do what it does today, and what would make it do less?

assessment.about: The "Assess your agent" page and its Claude review. One question per principle; each answer has three levels.

questions.question: How does work with the agent start?
answers: The user types into a prompt box or chat
There’s a summary or suggestions, but chat is the main way in
The agent starts on its own at the right moment and brings what needs attention
questions.why: If the user has to know what to ask, most of the agent’s value stays hidden.

fixes.title: Let the agent start the work
ideas: Start the agent on the dates and events the user already works to, such as time reporting closing, month-end or a client replying.
Open on what needs the user, each item with the problem, the proposal and the reason.
Lead with a recap of what happened and what needs the user, before any list.

fixes.title: Make what needs attention the starting point
ideas: Make what needs attention the default view, not a tab next to chat.
Say what started the run, at the top: “Started when time reporting closed.”
Show what runs next, and when, with a way to pause it.

keep.title: The agent starts the work
keep.text: Keep starting on the dates and events the user works to, and keep the starting point focused on what needs the user.

questions.question: How is it decided what the agent may do on its own?
answers: Some actions need approval, but the user can’t see which or why
A visible level per task: routine work runs alone, pay and filings wait for a person, and it stops at the edge of its rules
questions.why: When autonomy isn’t predictable, the user either checks everything or trusts too much.

fixes.title: Set a level per task
ideas: Give each task its own level, Off, Suggest, Ask first or Auto, so routine work can run alone while pay waits for approval.
Keep payments, pay and filings off Auto, with a named person who approves them.
Show the current level on screen, next to the task, with what the agent will do at that level.

fixes.title: Make each level visible, and prepare before acting
ideas: Show the level on every task, and say why approval is needed.
For anything that leaves the company, let the agent prepare it. Nothing is sent until the user confirms.
When a case falls outside the rules, stop and hand it to a named person instead of guessing.

keep.title: Control matches what’s at stake
keep.text: Check the level of every new task before it goes live, and keep pay and filings off Auto.

questions.question: When the agent acts, what does the user see?
answers: A one-time “AI” banner or a confidence score
A lasting agent label on everything it did, the reason behind each step, and an honest account when something fails
questions.why: Without a label and a reason, the user can’t tell what the agent did, so they check everything. Saying it’s AI is also a legal requirement in the EU.

fixes.title: Label the agent and show the reason
ideas: Put a plain role name, such as “Payroll agent”, on every task, proposal and message, on screen and in the log.
Show progress per source or step while it works, with what was found and the rule behind it.
Announce each step to screen readers, with the agent named and what it’s working on.

fixes.title: Replace banners and scores with labels and reasons
ideas: Replace one-time banners with a marker that stays on everything the agent filled in.
Replace bare percentages with the rule or source behind each step.
When something fails, say what failed, why, what didn’t happen and what the user can do next.

keep.title: The agent and its reasons are visible
keep.text: Label every new feature the agent touches, and keep the reason one click away.

questions.question: Can the user step in while and after the agent works?
answers: No: once it acts, it’s done
They can stop it, undo from a log, or correct it somewhere else
They can accept, edit or reject each change in one step, undo where the result shows up, and take over at any point
questions.why: The user trusts an agent more when they know they can stop it, and know what can’t be reversed.

fixes.title: Add ways to step in
ideas: Show each change as before and after, with accept, edit and reject.
Add undo where the result shows up, with how long it’s still possible.
Say before acting what can’t be undone, such as payments once they leave the bank.

fixes.title: Bring control to where the work is
ideas: Move undo out of the log and onto the result: “Sent 09:30. You can undo until 09:40.”
Replace “Accept all” with a decision per change, and mark high-stakes fields such as a bank account.
Let the user correct one change in place, instead of in a form somewhere else.

keep.title: The user can step in at any point
keep.text: Give every new action a way to undo it, or say before acting what can’t be undone.

questions.question: What happens when something new or unusual comes in?
answers: It’s flagged only when an anomaly rule fires
New and unusual items are flagged with the reason, and when it’s unsure it asks one specific question with a best guess
questions.why: Agents drift towards the familiar. In PITA, the new supplier or the changed bank account is where the risk is.

fixes.title: Route the unusual to a person
ideas: Summarise routine work in one line, and list only the items that need judgement.
Give each item one card: the problem, the proposal and the reason.
Show how many items need the user, and an empty state when nothing does.

fixes.title: Flag what’s new, not just what’s wrong
ideas: Flag first appearances too: a new supplier, a new tax rule, a changed bank account.
When it’s unsure, ask one specific question with its best guess, instead of guessing, while the rest of the work carries on.
Check that flags don’t single out groups of employees, for example people on sick leave.

keep.title: What’s new gets flagged
keep.text: Review the flags now and then, so they stay about what is new to each case.

questions.question: How does the agent gain more autonomy over time?
answers: It’s fixed: it always asks, or it runs on Auto from day one
Someone changes the setting by hand, with no track record to go on
It offers more after approvals without changes, steps back after corrections, and pay and filings never move up
questions.why: Autonomy granted all at once is either useless or reckless. A track record is what makes more autonomy safe.

fixes.title: Let autonomy be earned
ideas: Keep an audit trail in plain language: who did each step, which rules were used, and undo from the log.
Count approvals without changes, for each task.
Start every task at Suggest, and move up one level at a time.

fixes.title: Base autonomy on the track record
ideas: Offer the next level after a set number of approvals without changes, and let the user say no.
Step back a level after corrections or reversals, and say why.
Recap what was approved without changes, what was caught and where the agent was unsure. Pay, filings and salary changes never move up.

keep.title: Autonomy grows with a track record
keep.text: Keep counting approvals per task, and keep stepping back after corrections.

verdicts.name: An assistant bolted on
verdicts.meaning: Expect the user to check everything the agent does, or not use it at all.

verdicts.name: Useful, not yet trusted
verdicts.meaning: The user will use it, but still check most of its work by hand.

verdicts.name: Trustworthy in parts
verdicts.meaning: Some workflows can run with a glance. Close the gaps before giving the agent more autonomy.

verdicts.name: Best-in-class
verdicts.meaning: On paper, this is ahead of every competitor we studied. Now prove it with measured acceptance.
